title: Enums with Match
story: You're building a text adventure game. The player types a direction — North, South, East, or West — and expects to see what's there. A long chain of if/elif works... but there's a cleaner way.
why: The `match` expression is purpose-built for enums — it's cleaner than chained if/elif and the compiler guarantees you handle every variant.
analogy: Match is like a train track switch. The train (your code) approaches, and depending on which track is selected (the enum variant), it goes to a completely different destination.
try_it: Add Northeast, Southeast, Southwest, and Northwest directions. Use `|` to pair them: Northeast|North => "Cold". Test all eight directions.
tips: Match is exhaustive — the compiler forces you to handle every variant
Use `|` to combine variants that share the same handler: `North | South => "Vertical"`
Match can be used as an expression that returns a value — assign it to a variable or return it
common_mistakes: Using `:` instead of `=>` in match arms — match uses arrows: `North => { ... }` not `North: { ... }`
Forgetting to handle every variant — the compiler will catch this, but it's a common surprise
Writing `Direction.North` inside match patterns — use bare variant names: `North` not `Direction.North`
